# From Gene-level Rankings to Set-level Evidence

Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) asks whether members of a predefined gene
set accumulate near the top or bottom of a complete ranked list more strongly
than expected under a chosen null model. It can detect coordinated, moderate
gene-level changes that may not produce many individually selected genes.

| Item | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Input** | A genome-wide signed ranking and predefined gene sets |
| **Set-level statistic** | A weighted running-sum enrichment score (ES) |
| **Primary reported scale** | Usually the normalized enrichment score (NES) |
| **Uncertainty** | A permutation or other justified null distribution |
| **Drivers** | The leading-edge subset encountered before the score's extreme |
| **Experimental unit** | The independent biological unit whose labels or residuals may be permuted |

“GSEA” sometimes refers loosely to many ranked gene-set methods. This note
describes the original weighted running-sum procedure. Other competitive and
self-contained tests can use different statistics and answer different null
hypotheses.

# Constructing the Enrichment Score

Suppose $N$ eligible genes are ordered from the largest to the smallest signed
gene-level statistic:

$$
g_1,g_2,\ldots,g_N,
\qquad
r_1\geq r_2\geq\cdots\geq r_N.
$$

Let $S$ be a gene set with $N_H=|S|$ members in the ranked universe. Choose a
weight exponent $p\geq0$ and define

$$
N_R=\sum_{g_j\in S}|r_j|^p.
$$

At position $i$, the cumulative hit and miss fractions are

$$
P_{\mathrm{hit}}(i)
=\sum_{\substack{j\leq i\\g_j\in S}}
\frac{|r_j|^p}{N_R},
\qquad
P_{\mathrm{miss}}(i)
=\sum_{\substack{j\leq i\\g_j\notin S}}
\frac{1}{N-N_H}.
$$

The running sum is

$$
RS(i)=P_{\mathrm{hit}}(i)-P_{\mathrm{miss}}(i).
$$

It starts and ends at zero. Set members increase the curve, with larger increases
for more extreme ranking statistics when $p>0$; nonmembers decrease it evenly.
The enrichment score is the signed extreme departure:

$$
\boxed{
ES(S)=
\begin{cases}
\max_i RS(i), & \text{if the positive departure is larger},\\
\min_i RS(i), & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
}
$$

With $p=0$, every hit has equal weight. The common choice $p=1$ gives more
influence to set members with large absolute ranking statistics. Larger $p$
concentrates the result on fewer extreme genes and should be treated as an
analysis choice, not a harmless display setting.

# Direction and Leading Edge

A positive ES means set members accumulate toward the top under the declared
ranking direction; a negative ES means they accumulate toward the bottom.
Therefore, “positive” has no biological meaning until the contrast and sign of
$r_j$ are stated.

For a positive score, the **leading edge** contains set members encountered up
to the running-sum maximum. For a negative score, it contains those from the
minimum to the bottom of the list under the corresponding convention. These
genes drive the score, but they are selected by the same data and are not an
independently validated mechanistic core.

# The Null Distribution Is Part of the Method

## Phenotype-label permutation

In the original two-class expression setting, phenotype labels are permuted
across samples. For each permutation, the gene-level ranking is recomputed and
so is the ES. This tests a sample-level null of no association between phenotype
and the expression profiles. It preserves the observed correlation among genes,
which matters because correlated set members can create more extreme scores than
independent genes.

Label permutation is valid only under the exchangeability created by the study
design. In a paired study, labels may be swapped within pairs rather than across
all samples. Blocks, repeated measures, family structure, batches, covariates,
and unequal assignment probabilities can require restricted permutations,
residual permutation, rotation tests, or another model-based calibration. An
unrestricted shuffle is not repaired by performing many permutations.

## Gene-set permutation and preranked input

When only one ranked vector is available, implementations often compare the
observed set with random gene sets of the same size. This competitive null asks
whether the set's ranks are more extreme than ranks of genes outside the set.
It does not preserve within-set correlation in the way phenotype permutation
does, and it is not the same inferential experiment.

GSEAPreranked uses gene-set rather than phenotype permutation. Its nominal
p-values and NES therefore need not match standard GSEA even when the observed
ranking and raw ES match. The input format does not determine whether the
gene-level statistic itself was valid; it must already reflect the experimental
design, nuisance covariates, and correct biological replication.

# Normalization and Multiple Testing

Raw ES values depend on gene-set size and correlation structure. GSEA scales an
observed ES by the mean magnitude of null scores of the same sign for that set,
producing a normalized enrichment score:

$$
NES(S)=\frac{ES(S)}{E_0\{|ES^*(S)|\mid \operatorname{sign}(ES^*)=
\operatorname{sign}(ES)\}}.
$$

The denominator is estimated from permutations. Consequently, NES changes with
the permutation type, number of permutations, dataset, and software settings;
it is not simply a universal effect size. A larger absolute NES indicates stronger
standardized enrichment relative to that analysis's null, not a fold change in
pathway activity.

The original procedure estimates false discovery rates by comparing tails of
observed and null NES distributions across tested sets. This is not automatically
the same as applying Benjamini--Hochberg to nominal set p-values. Report the
implemented procedure, the complete tested collection, and the number of
permutations. Very small permutation counts yield coarse tail probabilities and
unstable FDR estimates.

# Ranking Statistic and Gene Universe

A useful ranking statistic is signed, comparable across genes, and aligned with
the scientific contrast. A model-based $t$- or Wald statistic often combines
direction, effect magnitude, and uncertainty better than raw fold change. An
unsigned p-value mixes opposite directions. A product such as
`sign(fold change) * -log10(p)` can create extreme values and ties and does not
necessarily have a well-calibrated sampling interpretation.

The ranked universe should contain eligible, uniquely represented genes. Remove
features that could not be tested by a prespecified rule, harmonize identifiers
with the gene-set collection, and document how duplicate probes or transcripts
were collapsed. Excluding genes because their observed results are inconvenient
changes the reference population.

Ties make the order within a block arbitrary. If many genes share a score, assess
sensitivity to tie handling rather than adding unexplained random jitter. Very
small sets are unstable; very large sets are nonspecific. Minimum and maximum
set sizes should be declared before inspecting results.

# A Conceptual Walk-through

Imagine a ranked list of 1000 tested genes and a 40-gene interferon set. If many
set members have large positive treatment statistics, the running sum rises
rapidly near the top and reaches a positive maximum. That maximum is the ES; the
interferon genes encountered before it are the leading edge.

The observed pattern is then compared with patterns generated under the chosen
null. Under valid phenotype permutations, each shuffle reassigns treatment labels
at the experimental-unit level, refits the gene statistics, and preserves
gene--gene correlation. A positive NES with a small multiplicity-adjusted error
measure supports coordinated association of that set with the treatment contrast.
It does not show that all 40 genes increased or that interferon signaling caused
the phenotype.

# Experimental Units and the Upstream Model

In bulk RNA-seq, independent participants, animals, or cultures usually determine
the treatment sample size. Reads and technical libraries refine measurements of
those units but are not exchangeable treatment replicates. In single-cell studies,
cells are commonly nested within donors or specimens; permuting cell labels as
if each cell were independently randomized is pseudoreplication.

The ranked statistic should come from a model containing the planned contrast,
blocking variables, batch terms, and within-unit dependence. If phenotype
permutations are used, they must reproduce the actual randomization or sampling
scheme. When such permutations are impossible, a method designed for the fitted
model may be more defensible than forcing the original GSEA algorithm.

# Diagnostics and Sensitivity Analysis

| Question | Diagnostic or sensitivity analysis |
|---|---|
| Does direction match the contrast? | Inspect several known positive and negative gene statistics |
| Is one gene driving the score? | Plot the running sum and inspect leading-edge contributions |
| Are results weight-dependent? | Compare defensible values of $p$, including an unweighted analysis |
| Is the null design-valid? | Write the exchangeability groups and verify each permutation respects them |
| Are terms redundant? | Examine gene overlap and shared leading-edge genes |
| Are rankings stable? | Refit under reasonable normalization, covariate, and influence choices |
| Is Monte Carlo error material? | Increase permutations and compare tail estimates across seeds |
| Are annotations robust? | Repeat with a frozen alternative collection or version when justified |

Gene-set correlation and overlap mean that a cluster of related significant terms
may represent one underlying signal. Summarizing redundant terms is useful, but
the leading edges, original test family, and adjusted results should remain
available for audit.

# Statistical versus Biological Interpretation

Statistically, enrichment means that set membership is associated with position
in a ranked gene-level result more strongly than expected under the stated null.
The sign refers to the ranking direction, NES is null-standardized, and the error
measure describes a multiple-testing procedure across gene sets.

Biologically, the result is a hypothesis about a coordinated program. It may
reflect pathway regulation, cell-composition shifts, shared upstream control,
annotation overlap, confounding, or assay bias. Establishing mechanism requires
gene-level effect inspection, relevant tissue and time context, external
replication, perturbation, and orthogonal measurement.

# ORA and GSEA Answer Different Questions

| Feature | [Over-representation analysis](over-representation-analysis.qmd) | GSEA |
|---|---|---|
| Gene-level input | Selected list | Complete signed ranking |
| Information discarded | Rank and magnitude within selected/unselected groups | Original sample data in preranked workflows |
| Typical statistic | Overlap count | Weighted running-sum extreme |
| Key null | Random overlap conditional on list and set sizes | No phenotype association or random-set competitive null |
| Main sensitivity | Selection cutoff and background | Ranking statistic, weights, and permutation scheme |
| Driver summary | Overlapping selected genes | Leading-edge genes |

GSEA avoids an arbitrary selection boundary but is not uniformly superior. A
scientifically meaningful binary list may make ORA natural; a reliable continuous
ranking may favor GSEA. The chosen method should follow the question and available
design information.

# Common Failure Modes

- **Permuting technical units:** this understates biological variation; permute
  at the independent unit and respect blocks or pairs.
- **Calling NES a pathway fold change:** NES is a null-standardized rank statistic,
  not an abundance effect.
- **Ranking by unsigned evidence:** up- and down-regulated genes become mixed;
  use a declared signed contrast.
- **Ignoring ties and duplicate identifiers:** arbitrary ordering changes the
  running sum; document collapsing and tie sensitivity.
- **Interpreting every enriched label independently:** overlapping sets often
  recycle the same leading-edge genes.
- **Treating enrichment as mechanism:** association of ranks and membership does
  not establish causal pathway activation.

1. GSEA summarizes where set members occur in a complete signed ranking.
2. The phenotype-permutation and random-gene-set nulls are different and must not
   be described interchangeably.
3. NES is specific to the estimated null distribution, not a biological effect size.
4. Ranking, weights, set sizes, identifiers, annotations, and permutations all
   require prespecification and sensitivity analysis.
5. Valid inference depends on the upstream model and independent biological units;
   biological mechanism requires evidence beyond enrichment.
